strengths: The paper addresses an important computer vision problem and demonstrates feasibility on full ImageNet-1K across multiple synthetic-data budgets. Combining representative feature targets with class-specific BatchNorm matching is a practical extension of SRe2L.
Table I shows consistent improvements over the strengthened, replicated SRe2L baseline. Examples include 64.8% versus 54.2% on ImageNette at 10 IPC and 57.6% versus 54.4% on ImageNet-1K at 50 IPC.

Reporting both published and replicated SRe2L results, including the hyperparameter changes responsible for improved reproduction, strengthens the comparison. Three-run evaluations, component ablations, regularization sensitivity, and ResNet transfer experiments provide useful supporting evidence.

The high-level pipeline is understandable, and the manuscript appropriately credits its principal dependencies, including SRe2L, DeepInversion, the Cuturi–Doucet barycenter algorithm, and Python Optimal Transport.
weaknesses: The central mathematical contribution needs clearer positioning. Equation (4) approximates a single empirical distribution with a support-constrained distribution. With squared Euclidean cost and freely optimized masses, its unregularized objective reduces to feature-space k-means quantization. The paper neither discusses this equivalence nor compares against clustering targets under the same recovery procedure, leaving the claimed Wasserstein-specific originality insufficiently established.

The ablations attribute most improvement to class-specific BatchNorm statistics. In Table III, this modification raises ImageNette accuracy from 54.2% to 64.0%, compared with 64.8% for the complete method. Holding cross-entropy and class-specific BatchNorm fixed, adding the barycenter loss changes accuracy by only -0.1, +0.8, and +0.5 percentage points across the three datasets. These results support the combined system but provide limited evidence that Wasserstein matching is its decisive contribution.

The connection between the optimized distribution and the exported dataset is incomplete. Equation (3) and Algorithm 3 optimize atom masses, but Algorithm 1 exports only images, and Equation (5) matches support locations without using those masses. The manuscript does not explain whether weighted sampling or training preserves them. Matching the locations alone need not reproduce the computed barycenter distribution.

Important solver details remain unspecified. Section III-B describes entropy regularization, whereas the supplementary algorithms present unregularized transport problems. The actual regularized objective, regularization coefficient, initialization, stopping criteria, and solver configuration are missing, making the central computation difficult to reproduce reliably.

The efficiency claim has limited comparative support. Table IV reports only one configuration at 64×64 resolution on ImageNette, measuring an individual synthesis update. The supplementary 14-hour ImageNet figure helps establish feasibility, but there is no comparable accounting of teacher training, feature extraction, barycenter computation, recovery, and relabeling against the baseline.

The broader claims about metric superiority and generalization exceed the evidence. There is no matched MMD-versus-Wasserstein experiment within the same teacher and recovery pipeline. Table II lacks baseline transfer results, so it cannot establish improved cross-architecture generalization. Likewise, t-SNE visualizations using representations trained on mixtures containing the synthetic data do not establish reduced reliance on background shortcuts.
